exam.name: Implementing End-to-End Security Controls for Cloud and AI Workloads

questions.topic: PIM — eligible vs active assignments and MFA on activation
questions.question: Contoso wants all Global Administrator access to be just-in-time. The CISO requires that (1) administrators must perform MFA at the moment of role activation (not earlier in the session), (2) every activation must be approved by another administrator, and (3) two cloud-only break-glass accounts must always work without going through PIM. Which configuration meets all three requirements?

options.A: Assign all administrators an active Global Administrator assignment with 'Require MFA on active assignment' and 'Require justification on active assignment' enabled in role settings, and exclude the two break-glass accounts from PIM management and from all Conditional Access policies.
options.B: Assign all administrators an eligible Global Administrator assignment with 'On activation, require Microsoft Entra MFA' and 'Require approval to activate' enabled in role settings, and grant the two break-glass accounts permanent active Global Administrator assignments outside PIM.
options.C: Assign all administrators an eligible Global Administrator assignment with 'Require MFA on active assignment' and 'Require approval to activate' enabled in role settings, and grant the two break-glass accounts eligible assignments that have no expiration date.
options.D: Create a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA for the Global Administrator directory role, configure PIM to issue active time-bound assignments of 8 hours, and keep the two break-glass accounts permanently active outside PIM and excluded from that policy.

questions.rationale: Eligible assignments require activation. The 'On activation, require Microsoft Entra MFA' setting forces MFA at activation time (not at assignment time, which is what 'Require MFA on active assignment' does). 'Require approval to activate' satisfies the approval requirement. Break-glass accounts must be permanently active and excluded from PIM/Conditional Access so a misconfiguration can never lock you out.

optionRationales.A: Active assignments are always usable — there is no activation step to gate with MFA, so requirement #1 is not met.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Eligible + 'On activation, require Microsoft Entra MFA' + 'Require approval to activate' meets requirements #1 and #2; permanent active assignments outside PIM for break-glass satisfies #3.
optionRationales.C: 'Require MFA on active assignment' applies when an admin creates an active assignment, not when a user activates an eligible role. Also, break-glass accounts must be active (not eligible) so they always work even if PIM is unavailable.
optionRationales.D: Time-bound active assignments still don't require MFA at the moment of activation; the user is already in the role. Conditional Access enforces MFA at sign-in, not at role activation specifically.

references.text: Configure Microsoft Entra role settings in PIM
Manage emergency access accounts in Microsoft Entra ID
Plan a Privileged Identity Management deployment

questions.topic: PIM — approval lockout risk
questions.question: While hardening PIM for the Privileged Role Administrator role, an engineer enables 'Require approval to activate' but specifies no approvers, intending to use the default behavior. Currently every Privileged Role Administrator is eligible-only with no active assignments, and no emergency access accounts have been configured. What is the most likely outcome?

options.A: Activation requests are automatically approved after a short timeout because no approvers are configured, so administrators can still elevate.
options.B: The tenant is at risk of being locked out of the Privileged Role Administrator role because no one can approve activation requests.
options.C: Activation requests are routed to all Global Administrators in the tenant, including those with only eligible assignments, and any one of them can approve.
options.D: PIM rejects the role-setting change and displays a validation error stating that at least one approver must be selected before approval can be required.

questions.rationale: When approval is required but no specific approvers are configured, the active Privileged Role Administrators and Global Administrators become the default approvers. If all administrators are eligible-only (no active assignments) and no emergency access account exists, there is nobody currently in a role who can approve activation — producing a lockout. This is exactly the scenario the PIM docs warn against.

optionRationales.A: Approval is never auto-granted just because no approvers are listed — that would defeat the control.
optionRationales.B: Correct. With all admins eligible-only and no emergency access account, there is no active approver, so activation requests cannot be approved and the role becomes unreachable.
optionRationales.C: Default approvers are only those who are currently active in the role — not 'all Global Administrators' regardless of state.
optionRationales.D: PIM does not prevent the configuration; it is the administrator's responsibility to ensure approvers exist.

references.text: Configure Microsoft Entra role settings in PIM — Require approval to activate
Manage emergency access accounts in Microsoft Entra ID

questions.topic: Conditional Access — Authentication Strengths vs Require MFA
questions.question: Fabrikam must restrict access to a high-value finance application so that only phishing-resistant credentials (FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business, or certificate-based authentication) are accepted. Users currently access the app with the standard 'Require multifactor authentication' grant control, which also accepts SMS and voice. What is the simplest correct change?

options.A: Add a Conditional Access policy for the finance app that references the Authentication Methods policy so that SMS and voice are excluded only for that application.
options.B: Replace the existing grant control with 'Require authentication strength' and select the built-in 'Phishing-resistant MFA' strength.
options.C: Disable SMS and voice calls tenant-wide in the legacy MFA service settings page so that users cannot register those methods for any application.
options.D: Define a named location for the finance app's IP range in Conditional Access and block all clients that sign in from outside that range.

questions.rationale: Authentication Strengths let a Conditional Access policy require specific authentication method combinations — the built-in 'Phishing-resistant MFA' strength restricts the satisfying methods to FIDO2 keys, Windows Hello for Business, and certificate-based authentication. The classic 'Require multifactor authentication' grant control accepts any MFA method registered by the user, including SMS/voice.

optionRationales.A: Authentication Methods policy registration scope does not target a single app; you cannot enforce per-app method requirements there.
optionRationales.B: Correct. The built-in Phishing-resistant MFA authentication strength is the supported way to require a specific MFA method per app/policy.
optionRationales.C: Disabling SMS tenant-wide is over-broad; other apps may still accept SMS for legitimate users. And it does not differentiate per app.
optionRationales.D: Named locations control where users can sign in from, not which MFA methods they used.

references.text: Conditional Access authentication strength
Conditional Access grant controls

questions.topic: Conditional Access — blocking legacy authentication
questions.question: A security review of Microsoft 365 sign-in logs shows hundreds of failed sign-ins per day using IMAP and POP3 against a handful of service mailboxes. Microsoft attributes the vast majority of password-spray success to legacy protocols. Which configuration most directly eliminates this attack surface for the entire tenant while preserving modern Outlook and Teams clients?

options.A: Disable IMAP and POP3 on each service mailbox individually by using Exchange Online mailbox protocol settings, and rotate every service-account password monthly through a scheduled runbook.
options.B: Create a Conditional Access policy targeting All users, All resources, with Client apps condition set to 'Exchange ActiveSync clients' and 'Other clients', and grant control set to Block.
options.C: Create a Conditional Access policy for All users and All resources that grants access only when MFA is satisfied, and rely on legacy protocol clients failing the MFA requirement.
options.D: Enable Security Defaults and rely on the built-in legacy authentication block, even though the tenant has custom Conditional Access policies already in production.

questions.rationale: The supported pattern to block legacy authentication tenant-wide is a Conditional Access policy with Client apps = 'Exchange ActiveSync clients' + 'Other clients' (the legacy bucket) and grant = Block. This catches IMAP, POP3, SMTP AUTH, and other non-modern-auth protocols regardless of which user/mailbox they target.

optionRationales.A: Per-mailbox blocks scale poorly and don't address other protocols (SMTP AUTH) or new mailboxes.
optionRationales.B: Correct. This is the documented Microsoft-managed approach to blocking legacy authentication.
optionRationales.C: Requiring MFA does not stop legacy auth attempts — legacy protocols cannot perform interactive MFA, so requests just fail (still consuming sign-in attempts and risking lockouts), but does not enforce a clean block.
optionRationales.D: Security Defaults cannot coexist with custom Conditional Access policies — enabling them disables custom policies.

references.text: Block legacy authentication with Conditional Access
Microsoft-managed Conditional Access policies

questions.topic: Conditional Access — report-only mode
questions.question: An engineer drafts a Conditional Access policy that requires compliant device for all users accessing Microsoft 365. The change-control board demands evidence that the policy will not lock out any users before it goes live. Which approach satisfies the board while keeping the rollout reversible?

options.A: Enable the policy in Report-only mode for one week, then use the sign-in logs to review the policy result column before switching to On.
options.B: Enable the policy in On mode for a pilot group of 20 users for one week, review their sign-in logs, and then expand the assignment to all users.
options.C: Save the policy with 'Enable policy' set to Off and have administrators review its conditions and grant controls in the portal before enabling it.
options.D: Enable the policy in On mode with an exclusion group containing every user, and then remove users from the exclusion group gradually while monitoring sign-ins.

questions.rationale: Report-only mode evaluates the policy against every sign-in and records what *would* have happened (Success/Failure/Not applied) in the sign-in logs, without enforcing the result. This produces tenant-wide impact data without risk and is the documented way to validate Conditional Access changes before enforcement.

optionRationales.A: Correct. Report-only mode evaluates the policy on real sign-ins and writes results to the sign-in logs without enforcement.
optionRationales.B: Pilot rings limit blast radius but don't measure tenant-wide impact and cannot reveal effects on users outside the pilot.
optionRationales.C: Off policies are not evaluated at all — they generate no data.
optionRationales.D: An exclusion-everyone trick produces no enforcement and no Report-only data; it is not a supported pattern.

references.text: Conditional Access report-only mode

questions.topic: Conditional Access — break-glass account exclusions
questions.question: Microsoft recommends two emergency access (break-glass) accounts permanently assigned the Global Administrator role. Which exclusion pattern best preserves their ability to sign in during an outage of the tenant's identity providers, MFA service, or Conditional Access misconfiguration?

options.A: Exclude the break-glass accounts only from the policy requiring MFA; leave them subject to all other Conditional Access policies for auditability.
options.B: Exclude the break-glass accounts from every Conditional Access policy by adding them to a dedicated security group that is referenced in the Exclude list of each policy.
options.C: Place the break-glass accounts in a restricted-management Administrative Unit and exclude that Administrative Unit from every Conditional Access policy that targets All users.
options.D: Grant the break-glass accounts a Conditional Access exemption by having them activate an eligible 'Conditional Access exemption' role in PIM at sign-in.

questions.rationale: Break-glass accounts must be excluded from *every* Conditional Access policy, not just MFA — the next outage could be in any control (compliant device, named location, sign-in risk, etc.). The standard pattern is a dedicated security group used in every policy's Exclude list, plus monitored alerts on use.

optionRationales.A: If a non-MFA policy (e.g., compliant device) malfunctions, the break-glass account is still blocked. Exclusion must be universal.
optionRationales.B: Correct. A dedicated exclusion security group referenced in every policy's Exclude list is the documented Microsoft pattern.
optionRationales.C: Administrative Units scope role assignments, not Conditional Access targeting. Conditional Access has no AU-based exclude option.
optionRationales.D: No such 'exemption' role exists. Conditional Access does not have a PIM-activated bypass.

references.text: Manage emergency access accounts in Microsoft Entra ID
Conditional Access best practices

questions.topic: Conditional Access — risk-based policies
questions.question: Northwind has Microsoft Entra ID P2 and wants to (1) require a secure password change for users flagged as high-risk by Entra ID Protection and (2) require MFA for medium-or-higher sign-in risk. Which combination is correct?

options.A: Create a single Conditional Access policy targeting All users and All resources that grants access only after a secure password change and MFA are both completed, and trigger it when either user risk or sign-in risk is high.
options.B: Create one user-risk-based policy with grant 'Require password change' targeting High user risk, and one sign-in-risk-based policy with grant 'Require authentication strength: MFA' targeting Medium and High sign-in risk.
options.C: Configure the legacy Entra ID Protection user risk policy and sign-in risk policy in the Identity Protection blade with the same thresholds and controls, because Conditional Access is not used for risk-based enforcement.
options.D: Create a single Conditional Access policy targeting All users and All resources that requires both a secure password change and MFA on every sign-in, regardless of any risk level.

questions.rationale: User risk and sign-in risk are evaluated separately, target different events, and call for different remediations. The current best practice is to author them as two Conditional Access policies (user-risk and sign-in-risk), not to use the older Identity Protection policies. The user-risk policy requires a secure password change; the sign-in-risk policy requires MFA at medium-or-higher.

optionRationales.A: Combining grants in one policy uses AND semantics, applying password change even when only sign-in risk is elevated.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Two policies — one per risk type — with the appropriate grant control and threshold.
optionRationales.C: Microsoft has migrated Identity Protection risk policies to Conditional Access; the standalone Identity Protection policies are deprecated.
optionRationales.D: Forcing password change on every sign-in is excessive and not what the requirement asks for.

references.text: Require MFA for elevated sign-in risk
Require password change for high-risk users

questions.topic: Conditional Access — AI Agents (Entra Agent ID)
questions.question: A development team builds an autonomous agent that runs without a user present and calls Microsoft Graph as itself. The CISO requires that if Entra ID Protection flags the agent identity as 'high risk', it should immediately be blocked from accessing tenant resources. What is the supported way to implement this?

options.A: Assign the agent's service principal to a Conditional Access policy with grant = 'Block', and reference the agent risk condition in the Conditions blade.
options.B: Enable the Microsoft-managed Conditional Access policy 'Block high-risk agent identities', which targets workload identities and blocks those flagged as high risk by Entra ID Protection.
options.C: Add the agent's service principal to a security group, and in the app registration deny that group the Microsoft Graph application permissions it was previously granted whenever the agent is flagged.
options.D: Configure an Azure Logic App that runs daily, queries Identity Protection for risky workload identities, and revokes the agent's tokens and credentials when it finds one rated high.

questions.rationale: Microsoft now ships a managed Conditional Access policy template, 'Block high-risk agent identities', specifically designed to block agent identities determined as high risk based on Entra ID Protection's agent risk detections. It is part of the AI Agents Conditional Access template category introduced for Entra Agent ID.

optionRationales.A: There is no 'agent risk' condition you select manually — the protection is exposed via the dedicated template/managed policy.
optionRationales.B: Correct. The 'Block high-risk agent identities' Microsoft-managed Conditional Access policy is the documented mechanism.
optionRationales.C: Denying API permissions is a coarse, manual revocation — not a risk-driven control.
optionRationales.D: A custom Logic App is far slower and is not the supported pattern when a managed policy exists.

references.text: Conditional Access policy templates — AI Agents
Block high-risk agent identities (Conditional Access)

questions.topic: Passwordless authentication — choosing the right method
questions.question: Adventure Works is rolling out phishing-resistant passwordless authentication. A regulated admin group of 50 users must use the most portable phishing-resistant credential that works across Windows, macOS, and shared kiosks, and must be usable on any computer the admin happens to be working from. Which credential type best fits this group per Microsoft's deployment guidance?

options.A: Windows Hello for Business (cloud Kerberos trust), which is bound to a single Windows device.
options.B: FIDO2 security keys, which are portable across Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android devices.
options.C: Microsoft Authenticator push notifications, which require the user to approve a prompt.
options.D: SMS-based authentication with strong password complexity, delivered to each administrator's phone.

questions.rationale: Microsoft's phishing-resistant passwordless deployment guide explicitly recommends FIDO2 security keys for admins and highly regulated users who need a portable credential — they are phishing-resistant, hardware-backed, and work across Windows, macOS, and shared/kiosk devices.

optionRationales.A: Windows Hello for Business is device-bound to a specific Windows PC and is not portable across macOS or shared kiosks.
optionRationales.B: Correct. FIDO2 keys are portable, phishing-resistant, and the documented recommendation for admins.
optionRationales.C: Authenticator push is not phishing-resistant on its own; it does not meet the requirement.
optionRationales.D: SMS is the weakest method and is explicitly discouraged for admins.

references.text: Plan a phishing-resistant passwordless authentication deployment
Enable FIDO2 security key sign-in to Windows

questions.topic: Passwordless authentication — Temporary Access Pass (TAP)
questions.question: A new employee is being onboarded remotely. The organization wants the user to register a phishing-resistant credential (FIDO2 or Microsoft Authenticator passkey) without ever using a permanent password, and without an in-person handoff. Which method is designed for this scenario?

options.A: Send the employee a one-time SMS code to register for MFA with the phone number on file, and then ask the user to set up a FIDO2 security key at a later date.
options.B: Issue the employee a Temporary Access Pass (TAP) from the Microsoft Entra admin center; the user then signs in with the TAP and registers a passwordless credential.
options.C: Have the employee call the help desk to receive a temporary password and register a backup security question, then register a passwordless credential after the first sign-in.
options.D: Provision a smart card through Active Directory Certificate Services and ship the physical card to the employee along with the PIN needed to enroll the certificate.

questions.rationale: A Temporary Access Pass is a time-limited passcode that lets a user complete their first sign-in and register strong authentication methods (FIDO2, Windows Hello, passkey, certificate) without ever needing a permanent password. It is the documented passwordless onboarding mechanism in Microsoft Entra ID.

optionRationales.A: SMS introduces a password requirement and is not phishing-resistant.
optionRationales.B: Correct. TAP is the designed passwordless bootstrap for new users.
optionRationales.C: Temporary passwords and security questions reintroduce password risk and are not phishing-resistant.
optionRationales.D: Smart card provisioning works but is operationally heavy and not the simplest match for the scenario.

references.text: Configure Temporary Access Pass in Microsoft Entra ID
Plan a phishing-resistant passwordless deployment

questions.topic: App registrations — credentials (federated vs client secret)
questions.question: A GitHub Actions workflow needs to deploy to an Azure subscription using an app registration in Microsoft Entra ID. Security requires that no long-lived secret be stored in GitHub. Which app-registration credential type meets this requirement?

options.A: A client secret with a six-month expiration that is stored as an encrypted GitHub Actions secret and rotated by a scheduled workflow.
options.B: A certificate uploaded to the app registration, with its private key stored as an encrypted GitHub Actions secret and renewed before it expires.
options.C: A federated identity credential on the app registration that trusts GitHub OIDC tokens from the specific repository and branch.
options.D: A managed identity that is assigned to the GitHub repository and used by the workflow runner to request tokens for the subscription.

questions.rationale: Federated identity credentials let an app registration trust OIDC tokens from external issuers (GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, Kubernetes, etc.). The workflow exchanges its short-lived OIDC token for an Entra access token at runtime — no secret is stored in GitHub. This is the documented approach for keyless CI/CD to Azure.

optionRationales.A: A client secret in GitHub is still a long-lived secret in a third party.
optionRationales.B: A certificate private key in GitHub is also a long-lived secret.
optionRationales.C: Correct. Federated identity credentials remove the need for any stored secret in GitHub.
optionRationales.D: Managed identities can only be assigned to Azure resources, not to GitHub repositories.

references.text: Workload identity federation (federated identity credentials)
Configure a federated identity credential on an app

questions.topic: OAuth — application vs delegated permissions and admin consent
questions.question: A custom daemon needs to read all users' calendars in a tenant. The developer has chosen Microsoft Graph 'Calendars.Read' as an application permission. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Application permissions are delegated to the signed-in user, so any user who installs the app can consent on behalf of the tenant by accepting the prompt.
options.B: Application permissions require a Global Administrator or other appropriate admin to grant tenant-wide consent before the app can call Microsoft Graph.
options.C: Application permissions only take effect while a user is actively signed in to the daemon, because the access token is issued on that user's behalf.
options.D: Application permissions cannot be exercised through the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow and must instead be requested with the authorization code flow.

questions.rationale: Application permissions are tenant-wide and have no user context. They always require admin consent — typically granted via the admin consent endpoint or by a Global Administrator on the API permissions page of the app registration. They are used by daemons/services with the client credentials flow.

optionRationales.A: Application permissions cannot be user-consented under any circumstances.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Application permissions always require admin consent.
optionRationales.C: Application permissions are specifically for non-interactive scenarios without a signed-in user.
optionRationales.D: Client credentials flow is exactly how application permissions are exercised.

references.text: Developer's guide to permissions and consent
Grant tenant-wide admin consent to an application

questions.topic: OAuth — user consent settings
questions.question: The CISO is worried about users granting consent to malicious third-party apps that request broad Microsoft Graph scopes. The goal is to allow user consent only for low-risk permissions from publisher-verified apps and require admin consent for everything else, with a workflow that lets users request admin approval. Which configuration achieves this?

options.A: Disable user consent for applications entirely across the tenant and require every consent decision to be made by a Global Administrator, regardless of publisher or permission risk, and users would receive no way to request approval.
options.B: Set 'User consent for applications' to 'Allow user consent for apps from verified publishers, for selected permissions' (the low-risk classification) and enable the admin consent request workflow.
options.C: Remove all existing delegated permission grants from third-party apps and require developers to rely exclusively on application permissions that administrators consent to once.
options.D: Configure a Conditional Access policy for All users and All resources that blocks every OAuth consent prompt presented by third-party multi-tenant applications.

questions.rationale: Microsoft Entra exposes a 'risk-based step-up consent' model: classify permissions as low/medium/high risk, allow user consent only for low-risk permissions from verified publishers, and enable the admin consent request workflow so users can ask for approval on anything else. This is the documented balance between usability and safety.

optionRationales.A: Disabling user consent entirely is heavier than necessary and creates help-desk overhead for benign apps.
optionRationales.B: Correct. This is the documented combination.
optionRationales.C: Application permissions don't fit the same use cases as delegated permissions; this isn't a replacement.
optionRationales.D: Conditional Access does not target OAuth consent prompts.

references.text: Configure user consent settings in Microsoft Entra ID
Configure the admin consent workflow

questions.topic: Managed identities — choosing system vs user-assigned
questions.question: A solution architect designs an Azure deployment where four VM scale sets need the same set of role assignments on the same storage account and key vault, and the team wants to define identity and RBAC before any VMs are deployed. Which managed identity choice best fits?

options.A: Assign a system-assigned managed identity to each of the four scale sets after it is deployed, then grant the same storage and Key Vault roles to each identity separately.
options.B: Create a single user-assigned managed identity, grant it the required roles in advance, and assign the same identity to all four scale sets at deployment time.
options.C: Create one service principal with a client secret, grant it the required roles in advance, and configure all four scale sets to authenticate with that secret.
options.D: Rely on the default Azure subscription identity that every deployed resource inherits automatically, and grant the required roles to that identity at subscription scope.

questions.rationale: User-assigned managed identities have independent lifecycles, can be assigned to multiple resources, and can have role assignments configured before the consuming resource exists. This decouples identity/RBAC administration from resource creation and is the documented best practice when multiple resources need the same identity.

optionRationales.A: System-assigned identities are tied to a single resource and can only be granted roles after the resource exists, multiplying the role-assignment work.
optionRationales.B: Correct. User-assigned is exactly the pattern for shared identity across multiple Azure resources with pre-created RBAC.
optionRationales.C: Service principals with secrets reintroduce credential management — the whole reason managed identities exist.
optionRationales.D: There is no subscription-wide default identity inherited by resources.

references.text: Managed identity best practice recommendations
What is managed identities for Azure resources?

questions.topic: Managed identities — federated credentials for workloads
questions.question: An AKS workload running in a pod needs to authenticate to Azure Key Vault. The platform team wants to avoid mounting any client secret, Kubernetes Service Account token, or pod identity, and they want a documented, Microsoft-supported approach. Which mechanism should they use?

options.A: Use Microsoft Entra Workload ID with federated identity credentials linking the Kubernetes service account to a user-assigned managed identity.
options.B: Store the Kubernetes service account token as a secret in Key Vault and have the pod read it at startup to authenticate to the vault.
options.C: Use Microsoft Entra Pod Identity v1 (aad-pod-identity) with a node-managed identity, which is the currently recommended pattern for AKS workloads.
options.D: Mount a client secret from a Kubernetes Secret object into every pod that needs Key Vault access and rotate it with a scheduled job.

questions.rationale: Microsoft Entra Workload ID for AKS uses OIDC trust between the Kubernetes service account and a user-assigned managed identity via a federated identity credential. No secrets are stored in the cluster. AAD Pod Identity v1 is deprecated; Workload ID is its supported replacement.

optionRationales.A: Correct. Workload ID + federated identity credential is the current Microsoft-supported approach.
optionRationales.B: Storing the service account token in Key Vault inverts the trust relationship and doesn't grant Key Vault access to the pod.
optionRationales.C: AAD Pod Identity is deprecated; Microsoft directs customers to Workload ID.
optionRationales.D: Mounting secrets reintroduces credential management and violates the requirement.

references.text: Microsoft Entra Workload ID for Kubernetes
Use Microsoft Entra Workload ID with AKS

questions.topic: Enterprise applications — SSO protocol selection
questions.question: A SaaS vendor offers both SAML 2.0 and OpenID Connect federation. Contoso's mobile-first workforce needs single sign-on from the Microsoft Entra My Apps portal, and Contoso wants to provision and de-provision user accounts in the SaaS automatically from Entra. Which combination is correct?

options.A: Choose SAML 2.0 for SSO and SCIM 2.0 for user provisioning.
options.B: Choose OIDC for SSO and rely on JIT (just-in-time) provisioning via SAML attributes.
options.C: Choose password-based SSO with Application Proxy for both SSO and provisioning.
options.D: Choose SAML 2.0 for SSO and configure delta sync via Microsoft Entra Connect to provision users to the SaaS.

questions.rationale: For non-Microsoft SaaS apps, SAML 2.0 (or OIDC) handles federated SSO, and SCIM 2.0 handles automatic user lifecycle (create/update/disable). Entra ID's enterprise application provisioning feature uses SCIM. JIT provisioning is a SAML-only fallback that creates accounts on first sign-in but does not handle disablement.

optionRationales.A: Correct. SAML/OIDC for SSO + SCIM for provisioning is the documented Entra pattern.
optionRationales.B: JIT cannot deprovision or update accounts; only create on first sign-in.
optionRationales.C: Password-based SSO stores credentials and is a fallback for apps that support nothing else; not relevant when SAML/OIDC is available.
optionRationales.D: Microsoft Entra Connect synchronizes on-premises AD to Entra ID — not Entra to SaaS apps.

references.text: Plan a SaaS application provisioning deployment (SCIM)
Single sign-on options in Microsoft Entra ID

questions.topic: PIM for Groups — role-assignable groups
questions.question: An organization wants to grant just-in-time membership in a security group that owns several Azure resource role assignments. They enable PIM for Groups. Which constraint applies?

options.A: Any Microsoft 365 or security group can be onboarded into PIM for Groups without special configuration, including groups that hold Microsoft Entra directory role assignments, and the group's membership type does not matter, and the group can also be nested inside other groups.
options.B: To assign Entra ID roles via the group, the group must be created with 'Microsoft Entra roles can be assigned to the group' enabled, which makes it a role-assignable group; role-assignable groups cannot contain nested groups.
options.C: PIM for Groups requires only the Microsoft Entra ID Free tier and works on any security or Microsoft 365 group without additional licensing or role-assignable configuration.
options.D: PIM for Groups cannot be used to grant Azure resource role access; it can only manage Microsoft Entra directory role access and cannot control group ownership or membership.

questions.rationale: Role-assignable groups have special protections and constraints: they must be flagged at creation, and they cannot have other groups nested inside them. PIM for Groups requires Entra ID P2 or ID Governance licensing.

optionRationales.A: Not every group qualifies; role-assignable groups have specific creation requirements.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Role-assignable groups must be flagged at creation and cannot be nested.
optionRationales.C: PIM (and PIM for Groups) requires Entra ID P2 or Entra ID Governance.
optionRationales.D: PIM for Groups can grant access to Azure resource roles, Entra directory roles, and group membership/ownership.

references.text: PIM for Groups overview
Use Microsoft Entra groups to manage role assignments

questions.topic: App registrations — redirect URI hygiene
questions.question: A developer registers a public client (native) mobile app. Which redirect URI configuration is the secure, supported choice for a mobile app using MSAL?

options.A: https://localhost:8080 registered as a Web redirect URI on the app registration, because the same loopback address works on every developer machine and emulator without extra configuration, which the MSAL library also accepts as a default.
options.B: A platform-specific redirect URI (iOS: msauth.<bundle-id>://auth; Android: msauth://<package>/<signature-hash>) set as a Mobile and desktop applications redirect URI on the app registration.
options.C: A wildcard redirect URI such as https://*.contoso.com registered on the app registration, so the app works from any subdomain without further configuration.
options.D: https://login.microsoftonline.com, so that the authorization code is returned directly to Microsoft's own sign-in endpoint for the app to retrieve.

questions.rationale: Mobile apps use platform-specific URI schemes registered as 'Mobile and desktop applications' redirect URIs in Microsoft Entra. MSAL libraries generate these automatically based on bundle ID / package name + signature. Wildcards are not supported and would be insecure.

optionRationales.A: https://localhost is appropriate for desktop loopback, not mobile apps.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Platform-specific URIs are the documented configuration for mobile clients with MSAL.
optionRationales.C: Wildcard redirect URIs are not allowed in Entra app registrations.

questions.topic: Key Vault — RBAC vs legacy access policy permission model
questions.question: A security engineer audits a Key Vault and finds that any user with the Contributor role on the subscription can grant themselves data-plane access to keys and secrets. The vault is using the access policy permission model. Which change addresses the privilege-escalation risk without breaking legitimate applications using managed identities?

options.A: Remove the Contributor role from all users at the subscription scope and replace it with Reader, so that nobody can change management-plane settings on the vault.
options.B: Migrate the vault to the Azure RBAC permission model so data-plane access requires explicit role assignments (such as Key Vault Secrets User) that only Owner or User Access Administrator can grant.
options.C: Add a deny assignment to the Key Vault that prevents Contributors from editing access policies, and keep the access policy permission model in place for managed identities, and rely on those deny assignments to block privilege escalation.

The Azure RBAC permission model uses standard RBAC roles for data-plane operations — Contributor cannot grant Key Vault data roles; only Owner or User Access Administrator can. Apps using managed identities continue to work once they are granted the equivalent RBAC roles.

optionRationales.A: Removing Contributor wholesale is over-broad and breaks legitimate management operations.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Migrating to the RBAC permission model is the documented fix for this exact escalation path.

questions.topic: Azure Policy — DeployIfNotExists vs Modify
questions.question: A governance team wants new Azure SQL servers to automatically have Microsoft Entra-only authentication enabled when created, applied as part of policy evaluation rather than via a remediation task. They want the resource property to be set during the create/update request. Which policy effect is appropriate?

options.A: deployIfNotExists — triggers a template deployment after the resource is created if a related resource is missing.
options.B: modify — adds, updates, or removes properties or tags on the resource during the create/update request itself.
options.C: audit — flags the SQL server as non-compliant when Entra-only authentication is off, but takes no corrective action.
options.D: deny — blocks creation of any SQL server that does not already have Entra-only authentication enabled in the request.

questions.rationale: The `modify` effect operates during the create/update request and can add, update, or remove resource properties (commonly tags, but also other supported aliases). `deployIfNotExists` is for ensuring a *related* resource exists (e.g., a diagnostic setting) and runs after the create returns success — not appropriate for setting a property on the same resource at creation time.

optionRationales.A: `deployIfNotExists` is for related resources and requires a remediation task for existing resources.
optionRationales.B: Correct. `modify` patches resource properties as part of the request itself.
optionRationales.C: `audit` only flags compliance state.

questions.question: A team must roll out an Azure Policy with a 'deny' effect across hundreds of production subscriptions, but they want to canary first in one region and progressively expand. Which approach matches Microsoft's safe deployment guidance?

The canary pattern starts narrow with no enforcement, validates compliance, then progressively expands selectors and switches to Default enforcement.

optionRationales.B: Correct. enforcementMode + resourceSelectors is the documented safe deployment approach.

questions.topic: Azure resource locks — ReadOnly vs Delete (CanNotDelete)
questions.question: A production storage account holds critical data. An engineer applies a ReadOnly lock to prevent accidental modification. After applying it, a developer reports that they can no longer list the keys for the storage account, which an application depends on. What explains the behavior and which alternative addresses the original goal without breaking key listing?

options.A: ReadOnly locks block all data-plane operations on the account, including key-based access to blobs; remove the lock and use Azure RBAC role assignments to prevent edits while keeping key listing available, which avoids any impact on the application's key retrieval.
options.B: ReadOnly locks block all writes, and list-keys is a POST that Azure Resource Manager treats as a write. Use a CanNotDelete lock instead, which prevents accidental deletion while still allowing management operations such as listing keys.
options.C: ReadOnly locks block data-plane read operations on storage, so applications and users cannot read blobs or list keys until the lock is removed; switch to a CanNotDelete lock to restore access.
options.D: The lock has not finished propagating across all Azure Resource Manager endpoints, so the list-keys call is still being rejected; wait 24 hours, retry, and only then consider changing the lock type.

questions.rationale: Azure Resource Manager implements list-keys for storage accounts as a POST operation, which Resource Manager classifies as a write — and ReadOnly locks block all writes (including POSTs that are technically reads). If the goal is to prevent deletion (the most common goal of locking critical resources), CanNotDelete is the appropriate lock and still allows management operations.

optionRationales.A: ReadOnly affects ARM control-plane writes, not data-plane reads on storage.
optionRationales.B: Correct. This is a well-known ReadOnly-lock gotcha; CanNotDelete is the right choice for delete protection.
optionRationales.C: Data-plane reads on storage are not gated by resource locks.
optionRationales.D: Locks apply immediately; this is a behavioral issue, not propagation.

questions.topic: Azure RBAC — custom roles

options.B: Actions includes 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/start/action' and '.../deallocate/action'; AssignableScopes is set to the resource group's resource ID.

options.D: Actions includes 'Microsoft.Compute/*'; AssignableScopes is set to the management group above the subscription so the role can be reused.

optionRationales.B: Correct. Specific action verbs + appropriate AssignableScopes.
optionRationales.C: Data actions are for data-plane operations (e.g., blob read); VM control operations are management-plane Actions.
optionRationales.D: Wildcards over-grant; assignable scope should match the intended use.

options.A: Key Vault Premium tier, which provides FIPS 140-3 Level 3 protection for HSM-backed keys.
options.B: Azure Managed HSM — single-tenant, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated, dedicated HSM pool.
options.C: Azure Dedicated HSM, which provides single-tenant hardware that Microsoft fully manages.
options.D: A customer-managed key in Standard Key Vault with a documented manual rotation process.

questions.rationale: Azure Managed HSM is a single-tenant, FIPS 140-3 Level 3-validated HSM-as-a-service. Standard and Premium Key Vault provide FIPS 140-2 (Premium is Level 3, Standard is Level 2). Dedicated HSM is a customer-managed bare-metal HSM, not Microsoft-managed.

optionRationales.A: Key Vault Premium is FIPS 140-2 Level 3, not 140-3.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Managed HSM is FIPS 140-3 Level 3 and single-tenant.
optionRationales.C: Dedicated HSM is customer-managed; the scenario says it should be managed by Microsoft.
optionRationales.D: FIPS validation level depends on the HSM, not on key management practice.

questions.topic: Microsoft Entra Permissions Management — overprivileged identities
questions.question: A multi-cloud environment (Azure, AWS, GCP) has thousands of identities. The CISO wants to identify identities with permissions they have never used and right-size them. Which Microsoft product fits this requirement?

options.A: Microsoft Defender CSPM with attack path analysis, which maps privileged identities across clouds and recommends removing the permissions each identity has never used.
options.B: Entra Permissions Management (CIEM), which finds identities across Azure/AWS/GCP, scores them with a Permission Creep Index, and recommends least-privilege roles based on usage.
options.C: Microsoft Sentinel UEBA notebooks, which baseline identity behavior across the connected clouds and recommend right-sized permissions for identities that never use them, and surface the results in the Sentinel investigation graph.
options.D: Microsoft Defender for Identity, which monitors identity signals across hybrid environments and recommends removing permissions that identities have never used.

questions.rationale: Microsoft Entra Permissions Management is the Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM) product for multi-cloud. It computes a Permission Creep Index (PCI) per identity and recommends right-sized custom roles based on observed activity over a tunable window.

optionRationales.A: Defender CSPM surfaces attack paths but does not analyze unused permissions per identity across clouds.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Permissions Management is the dedicated CIEM solution.
optionRationales.C: Sentinel UEBA focuses on anomalous behavior detection, not entitlement right-sizing.
optionRationales.D: Defender for Identity protects on-premises AD/Entra Connect from credential-based threats; it is not a CIEM.

references.text: What is Microsoft Entra Permissions Management?

questions.topic: Conditional Access — terms of use & step-up
questions.question: A regulated app requires (1) all access to be from a managed device, (2) MFA, and (3) the user accepts a Terms of Use document annually. Which Conditional Access configuration meets this?

options.A: One policy for the app with grant controls Require compliant device AND Require MFA AND Require terms of use, referencing the published Terms of Use.
options.B: Three separate Conditional Access policies, one per control, each configured to Block access when the user fails that single requirement.
options.C: A sign-in frequency policy set to every 1 year, combined with device compliance, so users must reauthenticate and accept the terms annually.
options.D: An authentication strength policy that includes Terms of Use as one of the allowed methods alongside compliant device and MFA requirements.

questions.rationale: Conditional Access supports combining grant controls (Require compliant device, Require MFA, Require terms of use) in a single policy with AND semantics. Terms of Use objects can be published in Entra ID Governance and referenced from CA — they re-prompt the user per the configured frequency.

optionRationales.A: Correct. A single combined policy with AND semantics matches the requirement.
optionRationales.B: Multiple block-on-failure policies is harder to reason about and not the documented pattern.
optionRationales.C: Sign-in frequency controls re-authentication, not Terms acceptance.
optionRationales.D: Authentication Strengths cover authentication methods, not Terms of Use.

questions.topic: Storage — user delegation SAS vs service/account SAS
questions.question: An engineer needs to generate short-lived, revocable SAS URLs for blob downloads from a web app. Auditing should attribute SAS-creation actions to specific Microsoft Entra users, and the storage account key must not be deployed to the web app's compute. Which SAS type meets all requirements?

options.A: Account SAS signed with the storage account key, which the web app retrieves from configuration at startup and uses to mint download URLs.
options.B: Service SAS signed with the storage account key and tied to a stored access policy, so each download URL can be revoked by editing the policy.
options.C: User delegation SAS, signed with a user delegation key that the web app's managed identity obtains using a role with the generateUserDelegationKey permission.
options.D: Shared Key authorization in which the web app signs every download request with HMAC-SHA256 using the storage account key held in its configuration, without issuing a SAS token to the browser.

questions.rationale: User delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key obtained from Microsoft Entra rather than with the storage account key. The SAS is attributed to the Entra principal that requested the key (the web app's managed identity), is revocable by revoking the user delegation key or the principal's role assignment, and never exposes the account key to the application. This is Microsoft's recommended SAS pattern.

optionRationales.A: Account SAS uses the storage account key — directly contradicts the no-key-deployment requirement.
optionRationales.B: Service SAS also uses the storage account key.
optionRationales.C: Correct. User delegation SAS is the documented, preferred pattern.
optionRationales.D: Shared Key authorization is not a SAS and also requires the account key.

references.text: Grant limited access to Storage resources using SAS
Create a user delegation SAS

questions.topic: Storage — disallow Shared Key authorization
questions.question: A security team wants to ensure that NO request to a storage account can succeed using the account key (Shared Key) — all access must use Microsoft Entra ID. Which configuration achieves this with the least operational complexity?

options.A: Rotate the storage account keys every 24 hours with a Logic App so that any leaked key becomes invalid within a day, and distribute the new keys through Key Vault.
options.B: Set 'Allow Shared Key access' to Disabled on the storage account so Shared Key authorization is rejected at the data plane, regardless of who possesses the key.
options.C: Assign an Azure Policy that audits Shared Key requests recorded in the storage diagnostic logs and raises an alert to the security team for each one.
options.D: Delete both storage account keys from the account so that no Shared Key credential remains available to authorize any request.

questions.rationale: Setting 'Allow Shared Key access' to Disabled on the storage account (control-plane property) causes the data plane to reject any Shared Key request and any service-or-account SAS (since those are signed with the account key). Only Microsoft Entra-authorized requests and user delegation SAS continue to work.

optionRationales.A: Rotation doesn't prevent use during the validity window.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Disabling Shared Key access is the supported, declarative control.
optionRationales.C: Auditing detects after the fact but does not prevent.
optionRationales.D: Deleting both keys breaks the account and blocks all rotation paths.

references.text: Prevent Shared Key authorization for an Azure Storage account

questions.topic: Storage — firewall, service endpoint, private endpoint
questions.question: A storage account holds data for an Azure Function in the same region. Security requires that traffic between the Function and the storage account never traverse the public internet, that no public endpoint exists, and that the account's public DNS name still resolves so existing on-prem clients (during migration) don't break. Which design meets all requirements?

options.A: Add a service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on the Function's subnet and a storage firewall rule allowing only that subnet, while leaving public network access enabled for selected networks, and add the Function's outbound IP addresses to the same firewall.
options.B: Disable public network access, add private endpoints in the Function's subnet for the storage services in use, and link the matching privatelink Private DNS zones so the storage FQDN resolves to private IPs in the VNet.
options.C: Disable public network access on the storage account and add the Function app's outbound IP addresses to the storage firewall allow-list, keeping the public DNS name unchanged.
options.D: Move the storage account to the Premium SKU, which provides automatic private connectivity for same-region Azure Functions and removes the need for a public endpoint or any DNS configuration.

questions.rationale: Private endpoint + Private DNS removes public exposure (public access disabled) while preserving the public FQDN, which resolves to the private IP within the VNet via the Private DNS zone. Service endpoints leave the storage public endpoint reachable. Outbound IP allow-listing doesn't remove public exposure and is unreliable for Functions on Consumption.

optionRationales.A: Service endpoints don't remove public exposure.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Private endpoint + Private DNS is the documented zero-public-exposure pattern.
optionRationales.C: Public access disabled means even the function's outbound IP wouldn't reach the account without a private endpoint.
optionRationales.D: SKU choice doesn't enable private connectivity.

references.text: Use private endpoints for Azure Storage
Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks

questions.topic: Defender for Storage — malware scanning on upload
questions.question: A storage account receives files from external partners through a public upload form. The SecOps team must block malware before it can be downloaded by anyone else and prefers an agentless solution. Which Defender for Storage feature addresses this?

options.A: The classic Defender for Storage plan with hash reputation analysis, which compares the hashes of uploaded files against known malware signatures without scanning file content, and generate an alert only for known-bad hashes.
options.B: Defender for Storage (new plan) with malware scanning, which scans each uploaded blob with Microsoft Defender Antivirus, records the verdict in blob index tags, and can trigger quarantine.
options.C: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps file policies, which scan files uploaded by external partners and quarantine those that match malware or sensitive content detections.
options.D: A scheduled Azure Function that downloads each new blob and scans it with a third-party antivirus signature library, then deletes any blob that matches a signature.

questions.rationale: Malware scanning is the dedicated Defender for Storage capability in the new plan. It scans uploaded blobs agentlessly with Microsoft Defender Antivirus, emits results via blob index tags + Event Grid, and integrates with quarantine automation. The classic plan only does hash-based analysis (not full content scanning).

optionRationales.A: Classic hash analysis is signature-only and limited.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Malware scanning in the new Defender for Storage plan is the documented, supported solution.
optionRationales.C: Defender for Cloud Apps targets SaaS, not Azure Storage uploads.
optionRationales.D: Building your own with Functions is operationally heavy and lacks Microsoft's threat intel.

references.text: Overview of malware scanning in Defender for Storage
Defender for Storage overview

questions.topic: Defender for Storage — sensitive data threat detection
questions.question: Defender for Storage in the new plan offers sensitive data threat detection. Which statement most accurately describes what this feature does and what it depends on?

options.A: It encrypts blobs at rest with customer-managed keys stored in Key Vault, and raises alerts when containers holding sensitive data are not encrypted with those keys.
options.B: It uses the Sensitive Data Discovery engine from Defender CSPM to find containers holding sensitive data (Purview SITs and labels) and raises the severity of alerts on those containers.
options.C: It performs real-time DLP inspection on every blob download and blocks any transfer that matches a sensitive information type before the data leaves the account.
options.D: It requires Microsoft Sentinel to function, because sensitive-data findings are only generated by analytics rules running in a Sentinel workspace.

questions.rationale: Sensitive data threat detection is configurable in the new Defender for Storage plan. It leverages the agentless Sensitive Data Discovery engine (shared with Defender CSPM) integrated with Microsoft Purview SITs and classification labels. Alerts that involve resources holding sensitive data are prioritized accordingly.

optionRationales.A: Encryption at rest is unrelated; that's a Storage Service Encryption feature.
optionRationales.B: Correct. SDD + Purview integration is the documented mechanism.
optionRationales.C: Sensitive data threat detection enriches existing alerts; it is not a real-time DLP enforcement.
optionRationales.D: Sentinel is optional, not required.

references.text: Sensitive data threat detection in Defender for Storage

questions.topic: Storage — blob immutability with time-based retention
questions.question: A regulatory requirement obligates a company to retain transaction logs unmodifiable for seven years. After commitment, the policy must not be shortenable by any administrator. Which Azure Storage feature meets this?

options.A: Soft delete with the maximum retention period, so that modified or deleted blobs remain recoverable for the full required window.
options.B: A container-level time-based immutability policy that is locked; once locked, retention can only be extended, never shortened or removed.
options.C: The Premium block blob tier, which provides low-latency storage and keeps the transaction logs on high-performance disks for seven years, with a hot access tier for the most recent logs.
options.D: A CanNotDelete resource lock on the storage account, so that nobody can delete the account or its containers during the retention period.

questions.rationale: Time-based immutability for blob containers enforces WORM semantics. The policy can be in an 'unlocked' (test) state initially and then 'locked' — once locked, the retention period cannot be shortened or removed and the policy cannot be deleted. This is the documented WORM/compliance feature for blobs.

optionRationales.A: Soft delete prevents accidental deletion within a window but does not prevent modification or shortening.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Locked time-based retention policy provides WORM.
optionRationales.C: Storage tier affects performance/cost, not immutability.
optionRationales.D: Locks prevent control-plane operations on the resource, not data-plane modifications.

references.text: Immutable storage with time-based retention policies
Set and manage immutability policies

questions.topic: Storage — encryption with customer-managed keys
questions.question: A storage account must be encrypted with a key the customer controls; key rotation must be automatic with no downtime, and the key vault should be isolated from the storage account's subscription. Which configuration meets this?

options.A: Use customer-managed keys with a versionless key URI to a Key Vault in a separate subscription, give the storage account's user-assigned identity the Crypto Service Encryption User role, and auto-rotate with a Key Vault rotation policy.
options.B: Use Microsoft-managed keys, which Microsoft rotates automatically at no cost, and rely on the platform to keep the encryption key isolated in a separate subscription from the storage account.
options.C: Store the customer-managed key in a Key Vault in the same subscription as the storage account, because Key Vaults in other subscriptions cannot be referenced for storage encryption, and auto-rotate it. The vault then needs its own private endpoint in that subscription.
options.D: Use customer-managed keys with a specific key version URI and rotate the key manually every 90 days by editing the storage account's encryption settings, giving the customer full control.

questions.rationale: Storage CMK supports a versionless key URI; when Key Vault's rotation policy rotates the key, the storage account automatically picks up the latest version without manual intervention. The user-assigned managed identity model allows the Key Vault to live in a different subscription. The 'Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User' role is the least-privilege RBAC role for this scenario.

optionRationales.A: Correct. Versionless URI + UAMI + Key Vault rotation policy is the documented zero-downtime auto-rotation pattern.
optionRationales.B: Microsoft-managed keys don't give the customer control over rotation.
optionRationales.C: Cross-subscription Key Vault is supported.
optionRationales.D: Manual rotation is unnecessary and brittle when auto-rotation is supported.

references.text: Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption

questions.topic: Azure SQL — TDE service-managed vs customer-managed key
questions.question: A company wants TDE on Azure SQL Database where (1) they can revoke key access to render the database inaccessible during an incident, (2) the key lifecycle (rotation, deletion) is fully controlled by the customer, and (3) no re-encryption of database files is needed when transitioning. Which configuration meets all requirements?

options.A: Service-managed TDE, where Microsoft manages the key lifecycle and key rotation, so no customer key vault is required to protect the database and no re-encryption is ever needed. The customer can still revoke access by deleting the database.
options.B: Customer-managed TDE (BYOK) with the key in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM; switching from service-managed only re-encrypts the database encryption key (DEK), so it is fast and online.
options.C: Always Encrypted with deterministic encryption, using a column master key in Key Vault so the customer can revoke access to the protected columns during an incident.
options.D: Disable TDE and use cell-level encryption with keys held in the database, so the customer can drop the keys during an incident to make the data unreadable.

questions.rationale: TDE with CMK (BYOK) gives the customer full lifecycle control of the protector key. Switching from service-managed to customer-managed only re-encrypts the DEK (fast/online) — the database files themselves remain encrypted with the same DEK. Revoking key access in Key Vault renders the database inaccessible.

optionRationales.A: Service-managed TDE doesn't give customer key control.
optionRationales.B: Correct. CMK BYOK satisfies all three requirements.
optionRationales.C: Always Encrypted protects specific columns; it is not equivalent to TDE encryption-at-rest.
optionRationales.D: Disabling TDE removes encryption at rest entirely.

references.text: Azure SQL TDE with customer-managed key (BYOK)
TDE overview for SQL Database and SQL Managed Instance

questions.topic: Azure SQL — Always Encrypted vs TDE
questions.question: A regulated workload requires that the database administrator cannot see clear-text values of credit-card numbers stored in a specific column — the data must remain encrypted at all times in the database engine, even during query processing. Which feature satisfies this?

options.A: Transparent data encryption with customer-managed keys in Key Vault, so the credit-card values are encrypted and the DBA cannot read them even while queries run.
options.B: Always Encrypted with secure enclaves; the column encryption key stays with the client driver, so the engine never sees plaintext and DBAs cannot decrypt the data.
options.C: Dynamic Data Masking on the credit-card column with a partial mask for unprivileged users, so DBAs only see masked values in their query results.
options.D: Row-level security on the credit-card table with a predicate that filters out rows for the DBA role, so DBAs cannot see the values in the column.

questions.rationale: Always Encrypted is the only Azure SQL feature that separates data owners (who can decrypt) from data managers (who cannot). The column encryption key resides on the client; the engine processes only ciphertext. Secure enclaves extend this to allow richer queries (range, pattern matching) while preserving the trust boundary.

optionRationales.A: TDE only encrypts data at rest — fully decrypted in memory and visible to DBAs.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Always Encrypted is the documented separation-of-duties feature.
optionRationales.C: Dynamic Data Masking only obscures values in result sets for unprivileged users; data is stored in clear text.
optionRationales.D: RLS controls which rows a user can see, not encryption.

references.text: Always Encrypted in Azure SQL
Always Encrypted with secure enclaves

questions.topic: Azure SQL — Microsoft Entra-only authentication
questions.question: A SQL Database server must reject all SQL authentication and only accept Microsoft Entra ID identities (users, groups, service principals, managed identities). Which configuration is correct?

options.A: Set the server admin to a Microsoft Entra group and keep SQL authentication enabled as a fallback for break-glass access, restricting SQL logins to a named list, with the SQL admin account monitored for sign-ins.
options.B: Enable 'Microsoft Entra-only authentication' on the logical server or managed instance; SQL authentication is then disabled for new connections, even for the SQL admin account.
options.C: Remove the SQL administrator login from the master database and delete every SQL login that has db_owner rights, leaving only Entra accounts in the server.
options.D: Apply an Azure Policy that denies CREATE LOGIN statements on the logical server so that no new SQL logins can be added, and keep the existing logins disabled.

questions.rationale: Microsoft Entra-only authentication is a server-level setting that disables SQL authentication entirely for new connections. Optionally combine it with an Azure Policy (Deny or Audit effect) to enforce it across all SQL servers/managed instances in a subscription.

optionRationales.A: Keeping SQL auth enabled defeats the requirement.
optionRationales.B: Correct. The dedicated 'Entra-only authentication' setting is the supported mechanism.
optionRationales.C: Removing the SQL admin login doesn't disable SQL auth for other logins.
optionRationales.D: Policies don't run inside the SQL engine; CREATE LOGIN happens internally.

questions.topic: Azure SQL — auditing destinations
questions.question: A SOC team needs Azure SQL Database audit events to be queryable in Microsoft Sentinel and retained for 1 year. The storage account that will receive the audit events is configured for Microsoft Entra-only authentication. Which configuration is correct?

options.A: Send audit events to Event Hubs only and forward them to Sentinel, because Sentinel cannot ingest SQL audit events from Log Analytics directly, and keep them for a year in the hub, with the hub's capture feature writing the events to storage.
options.B: Enable SQL auditing to a Log Analytics workspace (read by Sentinel) and to a storage account using managed identity authentication, since the account is Entra-only, with retention of 365 days.
options.C: Enable SQL auditing to a storage account and a Log Analytics workspace using the storage account keys as the authentication type, with retention set to 365 days.
options.D: Enable auditing only at the database level and not at the server level, because server-level auditing is deprecated, with the Log Analytics destination retained for 365 days.

questions.rationale: SQL auditing supports multiple simultaneous destinations: Storage account, Log Analytics workspace, and Event Hubs. When the storage account enforces Entra-only authentication, the SQL server's managed identity must be used (not storage access keys). Sentinel queries data already in its Log Analytics workspace.

optionRationales.A: Sentinel reads from Log Analytics; SQL audit can write directly to Log Analytics.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Multi-destination + managed identity for storage is the documented configuration.
optionRationales.C: Storage keys are not accepted when the storage account is Entra-only.
optionRationales.D: Server-level auditing is preferred for inheritance, not deprecated.

references.text: Set up auditing for Azure SQL Database
Auditing for Azure SQL Database — limitations

questions.topic: Defender for Databases — what's covered
questions.question: Which statement about Microsoft Defender for Databases is correct?

options.A: A single plan that covers Azure SQL, SQL Server on VMs, PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Cosmos DB at one flat price per subscription, enabled with one toggle and no per-plan configuration.
options.B: An umbrella of four separately priced plans: Defender for Azure SQL Databases, SQL Servers on Machines, Open-Source Relational Databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB), and Azure Cosmos DB, each enabled per subscription.
options.C: It requires a Microsoft Sentinel workspace, because database alerts and vulnerability findings are only generated when the plan is connected to Sentinel analytics rules for each engine. The plan would then be disabled whenever the workspace is deleted.
options.D: It is enabled automatically for every database when Defender CSPM is turned on, because Defender CSPM includes threat protection for database engines across the subscription.

questions.rationale: Defender for Databases is the umbrella term; it bundles four independent plans with separate pricing. Each plan can be enabled at the subscription level or on individual resources, and provides threat detection (anomalous activity, brute force, SQL injection) specific to that database type.

optionRationales.A: There is no single unified price; the four plans are billed independently.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Four plans, separately priced, enabled per subscription or per resource.
optionRationales.C: Sentinel integration is optional.
optionRationales.D: Defender CSPM is a separate plan focused on posture; it does not auto-enable database threat protection.

questions.topic: Defender for SQL — vulnerability assessment baseline
questions.question: Defender for Azure SQL Databases includes vulnerability assessment (VA). After the first scan, dozens of findings appear that the team considers acceptable for this database (e.g., a specific user permission that is intentional). How should the team prevent these from re-appearing as findings without globally suppressing the check?

options.A: Disable Defender for SQL on the database so that the vulnerability assessment no longer reports those findings, and enable it again after remediation.
options.B: Approve the current results as the baseline for those rules on that database; later scans compare against it and matching findings show as Pass.
options.C: Add a Defender for Cloud suppression rule that excludes the SQL database entirely from vulnerability assessment recommendations for the subscription.
options.D: Edit the vulnerability assessment rules XML to remove the checks that produce those findings, and redeploy the modified rule set to the database.

questions.rationale: VA in Defender for Azure SQL Databases supports per-database baselines: marking the current state as the baseline for a specific rule causes future scans to compare against it. Acceptable deviations show as Pass while genuinely new deviations from the baseline are flagged.

optionRationales.A: Disabling Defender loses protection broadly.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Per-rule baseline is the documented mechanism.
optionRationales.C: Suppressing the whole database loses too much coverage.
optionRationales.D: VA rules cannot be edited as XML.

questions.topic: Defender for SQL Servers on Machines — onboarding
questions.question: An on-premises SQL Server 2019 instance running on a Windows VM must receive Defender for SQL threat protection. The VM is already connected to Azure with Azure Arc. Which steps are required?

options.A: Install SQL Server on an Azure VM, migrate the on-premises databases to it, enable Defender for SQL on the new virtual machine, and then decommission the original instance.
options.B: Enable Defender for SQL Servers on Machines on the subscription holding the Arc-enabled VM; the extension deploys through Azure Arc and surfaces alerts and vulnerability findings in Defender for Cloud.
options.C: Forward the SQL audit logs to a Microsoft Sentinel workspace by using syslog and enable the Sentinel analytics rules for SQL Server threat detection on that workspace.

optionRationales.B: Correct. Arc + Defender for SQL Servers on Machines is the documented onboarding path.
optionRationales.C: Sentinel forwarding doesn't provide Defender for SQL's analytics.
optionRationales.D: Defender for Endpoint provides separate EDR protection.

questions.topic: Defender for Open-Source DBs — supported types
questions.question: An organization runs Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server and Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server. Which Defender plan should be enabled, and what does it detect?

options.A: Defender for Azure SQL Databases, which covers all Azure relational databases, including PostgreSQL and MySQL Flexible Servers, once it is enabled on the subscription and detects anomalous access.
options.B: Defender for Open-Source Relational Databases, which detects anomalous access such as brute-force attempts, behavioral deviations, and threat-intelligence matches for Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL (and AWS RDS).

optionRationales.C: Defender for Cosmos DB is specific to Cosmos DB, not MySQL/PostgreSQL.

questions.topic: Defender for Cosmos DB — what it monitors
questions.question: Which event would Microsoft Defender for Azure Cosmos DB most likely raise as a security alert?

options.A: An anomalous extraction of a large volume of documents from a Cosmos DB account by a previously unused identity, suggesting data exfiltration.
options.B: A failed Azure Resource Manager deployment to a Cosmos DB account caused by an invalid throughput setting in the template, repeated several times.
options.C: An expired primary read/write key on the Cosmos DB account that has not been regenerated within the past 90 days, leaving the account unusable.
options.D: A request to the Cosmos DB account from a well-known Azure datacenter IP address in the same region as the account, using a valid key.

questions.rationale: Defender for Cosmos DB detects suspicious data-access patterns: data exfiltration anomalies, suspicious access from rare locations or IP reputations, and key-misuse patterns. ARM deployment failures, expired keys, and Azure-internal IPs are normal operational events.

optionRationales.B: Deployment failures are not security alerts.
optionRationales.C: Cosmos keys don't expire automatically.
optionRationales.D: Azure datacenter IPs are not suspicious.

questions.topic: Azure SQL — Dynamic Data Masking
questions.question: An application returns credit card numbers to a CRM. Service representatives must only see the last four digits, while a small group of compliance analysts must see the full value for audits. Database admins should bypass the masking. Which feature meets this?

options.A: Always Encrypted with deterministic encryption, with compliance analysts given access to the column master key so they can read the full value through the same client driver.
options.B: Dynamic Data Masking on the credit-card column with a partial mask showing the last 4 digits, with the compliance analysts and dbo added to the unmasked users list.
options.C: Row-Level Security with security predicates that return the full row only to compliance analysts and database admins and hide the rows from service reps.
options.D: Cell-level encryption using symmetric keys in the database, with decrypt permissions granted only to the compliance analysts and the database admins.

questions.rationale: Dynamic Data Masking is presentation-layer masking — it changes what a query sees in the result set based on the principal. Admins (db_owner) bypass masking by default; analysts can be added to the exempted users list. Always Encrypted hides values from everyone including the engine, which is too strong for this dual-audience requirement.

optionRationales.A: Always Encrypted would prevent service reps from getting even the last 4 digits in plaintext.
optionRationales.B: Correct. DDM is the presentation-layer masking with exemption lists.
optionRationales.C: RLS filters rows, not column values.
optionRationales.D: Cell-level encryption requires application-side key management and doesn't address the dual audience cleanly.

questions.topic: Azure SQL — Microsoft Defender for SQL alert response (SQL injection)
questions.question: Defender for Azure SQL raises a 'Potential SQL injection' alert on a public-facing application. The alert details show vulnerable code constructed query strings with user input. What is the most appropriate immediate response and longer-term remediation?

options.A: Suppress the alert and accept the risk, because the database is restored from backup every night, the application only handles non-critical data, and no downtime is expected. The vendor can review the code during the next planned release.
options.B: Investigate the alert (identity, query, source IP), block an active offending source, and have developers move to parameterized queries or stored procedures, adding WAF rules in front of the app.
options.C: Restore the database from the most recent clean backup, re-enable the application so users can continue working, and schedule a review of the alert for the next sprint.
options.D: Enable Always Encrypted on every column in the schema so the injected queries return only ciphertext, leaving the application code unchanged and deferring any code review.

questions.rationale: SQL injection alerts indicate a real application vulnerability. The standard response is investigate scope and impact, block the active source if exploitation is occurring, then remediate by switching to parameterized queries and adding a WAF as defense-in-depth. Backups and Always Encrypted do not address the injection vector.

optionRationales.A: Ignoring is unsafe and not a response.
optionRationales.B: Correct. Investigate + active blocking + code fix + WAF is the documented full response.
optionRationales.C: Restore doesn't prevent re-exploitation.
optionRationales.D: Always Encrypted protects column values but doesn't fix the injection vector.
